reverse_outline.summary: Three-point digest: trust controls shift data, decisions and losses to other parties, each leaves a leftover with the business, and the linked leftovers need an owner
Opening case: a card-testing bot attack on one Larkfield studio cost fees and 31 hours of sales although Larkfield held no card numbers
The case refutes the add-it-and-have-it view of security; in payments a control assigns who holds data and who pays on failure
The part's thesis, spelled out control by control: what each of the five moves away and what it leaves with you
Why controls relocate rather than remove: each is a responsibility-assigning rule, and the rules interlock / the practical question to ask instead of "are we compliant?"
Limits of the evidence: Stripe and Adyen publish unevenly, and chapters flag where the record ends
Roadmap of the five chapters, ordered from credential to payer to paid business, each starting from a Larkfield case
Preview of the tokenization chapter: how vaults and tokens take card numbers and PCI scope off the merchant, and the payment page that remains
Preview of the network-token chapter: a network-maintained substitute number that survives card replacement, with incomparable vendor gain figures
Preview of the fraud chapter: the provider estimates dispute probability and blocks above a threshold whose cost the merchant bears
Preview of the 3-D Secure chapter: bank authentication of the payer, and liability shifting only when that check actually runs
Preview of the compliance chapter: seller verification as deadline-driven requirements that gate payouts, modelled as state
Reading guidance: each chapter maps to a question a reader may bring, and the recommended start is tokenization

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The AC-1 reader states the claim (controls relocate and leave a remainder, they do not remove risk) and names the five chapters' subjects in the expected order, each with what moves and what stays. The intro-only reader predicts the same five chapters in order, the three kinds of evidence (Larkfield cases, what Stripe and Adyen publish, the rules) and the tone.

After the KEY POINTS callout the page opens on the Card-Testing Weekend as an event with its figures (8-9 August 2026, 61,000 numbers, EUR 1 payments, EUR 4,100, 31 hours); no definition, placeholder or restated question.
12 of 12 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in spec order; the callout is aligned to nothing.

One unit marked two_ideas (Introduction ¶4). Ruled one idea: the reason (each control is a rule that assigns responsibility) and the question it leads to are one because-therefore line, as the spec's p04 declares. The sentence on linked rules inside it is ruled on under flow_is_followable.
The five chapter paragraphs tie to P5-1 to P5-5 one each; the six opening paragraphs and the closing one state, justify, bound or apply the same claim. No paragraph is untied.

Both figures carry a caption saying what they show; the Stripe quotation and the three rules in Introduction ¶4 follow the sentence that says what they show; each Larkfield case in the chapter list directly accompanies the statement it illustrates. The 41%/86% dispute figures are tied to their point only by the word 'later' in the same sentence, which is thin but sufficient.

11 of 11 boundaries express the declared relationship. At Chapters ¶4 the prose names the declared carried-over item (the risk rule's third action), but the page has not introduced it; that is ruled on under flow_is_followable.
'Where to Begin' does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic, holds no body evidence and does not end on a rephrased thesis; it ends on a course of action.
The conclusion returns to the opening weekend: 'The opening weekend returns in two of them, first as the control that worked and then as the attack that control was never about.'

results.quote: Each chapter answers a question you may arrive with: where card numbers may go, why a stored card kept working, why a payment was blocked, who carries a fraud loss, why a seller's payouts stopped.
results.finding: The conclusion synthesizes (chapters mapped to the reader's questions, the weekend seen from two chapters) but never says why it matters: the declared so-what (ask what stayed with the business and who owns it before counting a risk as handled) appears only in Introduction ¶4. The spec's p12 controlling idea is also silent on it, though conclusion.so_what declares it.

results.quote: bots tested 61,000 stolen card numbers with €1 drop-in payments through the public booking widget
results.finding: 'drop-in payments' reads as a payments term (a drop-in checkout component) in a payments book; both readers stopped on the page's first sentence and guessed that it means payment for a drop-in class.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 (flow reader A, item 3.1)

results.quote: 3-D Secure moves a fraud loss to the issuer, the cardholder's bank, only when the payer is authenticated.
results.finding: The other four sentences of the claim paragraph say 'moves X to Y and leaves you Z'; this one drops the remainder, so both readers had to infer it from the key points and Figure 2. The figure's 'Loss' tile then seems to belong to a different control than the text's 'leaves you the loss on what you accept' (risk score), and the difference between the two losses is not stated.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 6 (flow reader A, item 3.4)

results.quote: The rules are also linked: Stripe's PCI guide says its fraud tool is available only when its own client-side code collects the card.
results.finding: The paragraph is about rules that assign responsibility, and this example is a product condition that links two controls, not two rules (the key points say 'the controls are linked'). One reader re-read to find what 'linked' meant; the other read it as an afterthought and could not follow the step from this one link to 'so the question to ask is'.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2 and section 4, second suggested change (flow reader A, item 3.6)

results.quote: explains the risk rule's third action, between allow and block
results.finding: The link to the previous chapter rests on a 'risk rule' with three actions, which the page has not introduced: the fraud paragraph speaks only of estimating and blocking above a threshold. Both readers could not tell what the third action was. The spec's carries_over for p10 names it, but no earlier unit of the spec gives it; a clause in the draft would be enough.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 7 (flow reader A, item 3.8)

results.quote: this introduction makes no factual claim of its own
results.finding: Both readers stopped here: the opening states facts on its own authority (a Stripe quotation, what Stripe's PCI guide says, what European law does, what the two companies publish), so the sentence reads as a contradiction and as a second, different statement about evidence. It means that every fact here repeats one a chapter makes and cites, and does not say so.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 9 (flow reader A, item 3.7)

results.quote: Larkfield stored none of those numbers, and nothing was stolen from it.
results.finding: The weekend is not tied to the claim that follows: the prose does not say that a provider-served frame took the numbers (the first control at work) and that the page stayed, so one reader had to infer that the case is an instance of tokenization until 'Where to Begin' says so. Reported by flow reader B only (item 3 and section 4, first suggested change).

results.quote: A network token moves the stored card to the card network and leaves you a provider token behind which the card can change.
results.finding: 'network token' and 'provider token' (both on the does_not_know list) carry the thesis sentence with no gloss; the glosses come only in the chapter list. Both readers re-read the sentence and neither could say at that point what is left with the business.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item 3.5; flow reader B, item 5

results.quote: Larkfield cannot sign the script line of the shortest PCI form
results.finding: 'PCI' is used three times ('Stripe's PCI guide', 'the shortest PCI form') and never connected to 'the card industry's security standard', the name the page uses for it; PCI scope is on the does_not_know list. The AC-1 reader also noted that the page does not expand it.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, items 3.5 and 3.10; flow reader B, smaller points after item 9
